inhalt:
by Reinhard König, 2012

The category Urban Planning examines (simulation) models that can be used for urban planning purposes. This introduction sets out the aspects according to which models are evaluated in what follows. The DIKW (Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom) hierarchy is helpful for developing these criteria: its first step describes how information is generated from data by understanding the relations between them. If, in turn, one recognizes patterns in the information, one gains knowledge about a particular matter. In a final step, wisdom can be attained by understanding universally valid principles. Figure 1 shows this process as a diagram.

Figure 1: DIKW hierarchy. Reproduced after Bellinger, G., Castro, D., & Mills, A.: Data, Information, Knowledge, and Wisdom.

When models are used for urban planning tasks, it is crucial to gain knowledge about the effects of planned interventions in an urban system. A model is therefore always used in a specific context and, above all, with regard to a defined planning problem. Clarifying at the outset what a model is to be used for is essential in order to judge whether it makes sense to use a particular model at all, because using a model to support planning always requires resources. Here, resources primarily comprise money, time, and data. How large this investment of resources is depends above all on the complexity of the model. As a rule, more complex models also require more resources. As shown in Figure 2, this relationship can, in simplified terms, be assumed to be linear.


Figure 2: Relationship between the resources required and the complexity of a model.

If we turn to the question of how much knowledge we can gain from a model with what investment of resources, it first seems plausible that knowledge about a particular problem cannot be increased indefinitely merely by investing additional resources. As a simplifying assumption, we can posit a logarithmic relationship, as shown in Figure 3. It shows that different models allow different amounts of knowledge to be generated. Model a in Figure 3 is clearly the most effective model, since with it knowledge increases fastest as the investment of resources grows. Beyond a certain point, however, additional resources yield only a very small gain in knowledge for all models. To choose a model that is as useful as possible, one should therefore first answer the question: What kind of knowledge, and how much of it, is to be gained?


Figure 3: Relationship between the knowledge that can be generated and the resources required when using different models.

Let us now try to clarify the relationship between the investment of resources and the usefulness of a model. Figure 2 has already shown that the investment of resources can be equated with the complexity of a model. The assumption that, beyond a certain point, the knowledge gained from a model can hardly be increased by further resources leads us to the conclusion that between very simple and very complex models there is a range in which the most useful models are located (Figure 4).

Useful here means that a great deal of knowledge for solving a particular (planning) problem can be gained with as little investment of resources as possible, that is, with simple models. In the present context, it seems important to me to point out that the usefulness of a model has nothing to do with the accuracy of its results. On the contrary, too many details can distract from the information relevant to planning and thereby hinder the step toward knowledge.


Figure 4: The range of the most useful models. This range lies between very simple and extremely complex models.

In conclusion, on the basis of the considerations set out above, it can be stated that the usefulness of a model can only be meaningfully assessed if we are able to define a (planning) problem for which we want to use the model to gain knowledge or plausible approaches to a solution. To anyone working with models for planning purposes, we can therefore call out: Problems first!
